Get national, subnational or disaggregated data for almost 2000 indicators collected in more than 90 low and middle income countries.

Data:
The DHS Program API data are offered at different levels for individual implementations. The data are divided into four main levels:
- National Data: Provides specific indicator data at a national level. Users have the ability to query data for a particular country or group of countries for analysis and comparison (e.g. a researcher with a particular interest in child health across Kenya, Tanzania and Ethiopia could quickly query the national data and access data for all three countries).
- Subnational Data: Provides specific survey data on a subnational level allowing users to review data for regions within a specific country (e.g. a researcher reviewing and analyzing trends on infant mortality between the various states in India could query the subnational data and obtain this information).
- Background Data: Provides specific survey data on a categorical level. Users have the ability to query data for a particular category or categories for analysis and comparison (e.g. urban/rural, education and wealth level).
- All Data: Provides all the survey data available for the requested surveys and indicators. It contains a number of standardised indicators based on the central concept of "equivalised household disposable income", i.e. the total income received by the households less the current taxes and transfers they pay, adjusted for household size with an equivalence scale. While household income is only one of the factors shaping people's economic well-being, it is also the one for which comparable data for all OECD countries are most common. Income distribution has a long-standing tradition among household-level statistics, with regular data collections going back to the 1980s (and sometimes earlier) in many OECD countries.

Achieving comparability in this field is a challenge, as national practices differ widely in terms of concepts, measures, and statistical sources. In order to maximise international comparability as well as inter-temporal consistency of data, the IDD data collection and compilation process is based on a common set of statistical conventions (e.g. on income concepts and components). The information obtained by the OECD through a network of national data providers, via a standardized questionnaire, is based on national sources that are deemed to be most representative for each country.

Small changes in estimates between years should be treated with caution as they may not be statistically significant.

The SPI focuses on five key dimensions of a country’s statistical performance: (i) data use, (ii) data services, (iii) data products, (iv) data sources, and (v) data infrastructure. This will replace the Statistical Capacity Index (SCI) that the World Bank has regularly published since 2004.The SPI focus on five key pillars of a country’s statistical performance: (i) data use, (ii) data services, (iii) data products, (iv) data sources, and (v) data infrastructure.
